theme: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 95. Yesterday’s chapter described a generation that hardened its heart. Today’s psalm reads that story as a warning to us. Read it aloud, and notice the sudden change of tone in verse 7.
settingTheScene: Psalm 95 is a psalm of worship that has been sung in the church’s morning prayer for centuries. It starts with a joyful call to come and sing, and then shifts at the end into an urgent warning drawn from Numbers 14. The psalm does not name its author, but Hebrews 4:7 attributes it to David. The setting is the worship of the gathered congregation, who are reminded that praise must go with obedience.
observation: “Oh come, let us sing to the LORD; let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation!” (v. 1).
“Let us come into his presence with thanksgiving; let us make a joyful noise to him with songs of praise!” (v. 2).
“For the LORD is a great God, and a great King above all gods” (v. 3).
“In his hand are the depths of the earth; the heights of the mountains are his also” (v. 4).
“Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD, our Maker!” (v. 6).
“For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand” (v. 7).
“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah, as on the day at Massah in the wilderness” (vv. 7-8).
“Therefore I swore in my wrath, They shall not enter my rest” (v. 11).
interpretation:
The psalm has two halves, and the contrast is meant to startle us. The first half, verses 1 to 7a, is full of praise: singing, shouting, thanksgiving, bowing down. The second half is a warning. The same God who is a great king and a good shepherd is also the God who swore that a generation would not enter his rest. The psalmist places the two side by side because true worship includes both.

Worship, in this psalm, has an inward and an outward side. It is noisy and joyful, and it is also quiet and obedient. “Let us kneel before the LORD” and “if you hear his voice.” It is not enough to sing loudly. The test of worship is whether we listen.

The word “today” is the key. It is a present-tense word. “Today, if you hear his voice” does not refer to the past or the future. The wilderness generation heard his voice at Sinai and then refused. The psalmist says that the same opportunity is offered to every generation. It is as urgent now as then.

The phrase “do not harden your hearts” implies that hearts can be hardened or softened by our own choices. It is a process, not an event. Each time we ignore God’s voice, it becomes easier to ignore the next time. Each time we obey, our hearts become more sensitive. We are always moving in one direction or the other.

And “my rest” is the goal of the whole journey. The land was a picture of that rest, but the real thing is deeper: to be at home with God. The sad truth is that people can sing about it, and still miss it.
connection: Hebrews 3:7-4:13 is an extended meditation on this psalm. The writer applies it to Christians: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” He says that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, and “let us therefore strive to enter that rest” (Hebrews 4:9-11). Jesus invites, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).
application:
Read Psalm 95 aloud as an act of worship. Include the warning.

Ask whether there is a place where you have been ignoring God’s voice. Today is the day to listen.

Thank God that the rest he promises is found in Christ, and ask him to soften any hardness in your heart.
prayerPrompts: Tell God you want to hear his voice today.
Ask him to keep your heart soft and keep you from unbelief.
Thank him for the rest that is yours in Jesus.
